title: Is It Better to Have a Lot of Casual Friends or a Few Close Ones?
gist: New research published in Evolution and Human Behavior challenges the assumption that people must trade off between having many casual friends and having a few emotionally close ones, arguing the two are not a forced trade-off despite limited time.

insights.claim: With time squeezed by family, work, and chores, people often feel they must choose between having a few emotionally close friendships or many friends they are less invested in.
insights.speaker: Jessica D. Ayers
insights.so_what: States the conventional assumption about friendship quantity versus quality that the new research sets out to test.
insights.quote: With time as a limited resource, people often think they must choose between having a few emotionally close friendships or a lot of friends they’re less invested in.

insights.claim: New research by Jessica D. Ayers and Diego Guevara Beltran, published in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior, suggests people don't actually have to pick between having many friends and being emotionally close with them.
insights.speaker: Jessica D. Ayers
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the assumed necessity of a quantity-versus-quality friendship trade-off, with implications for how people think about allocating limited social time.
insights.quote: But our new research published in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior suggests people don’t actually pick between having many friends and being emotionally close with them.

insights.claim: The study specifically investigated what people prioritize when forming new friendships.
insights.speaker: Jessica D. Ayers
insights.so_what: Clarifies the study's focus is on friendship-formation priorities rather than existing friendship maintenance.
insights.quote: A new study investigated what people prioritize for new friendships.
